# mm

> A free, open-source command-line to-do list and habit tracker that shows you
> exactly one task at a time. While a "gate" is open it refuses to offer any
> easier work, which makes it an anti-procrastination tool rather than a task
> database.

Tagline: Never choose what to work on again.
Brand line: Decide what's next. Never when.
Homepage: https://mm.tafil.app/
Documentation: https://mm.tafil.app/docs (plain text: https://mm.tafil.app/llms-full.txt)
Source: https://github.com/Toseef-Ahmad/mm
Licence: MIT
Language: Python 3.11+, standard library only, zero runtime dependencies
Platforms: macOS, Linux (Windows untested; WSL works)
Install: pipx install git+https://github.com/Toseef-Ahmad/mm.git
Price: free, no account, no telemetry, no network code

## What it is

A single-user command line tool. Two commands do the daily work: `mm` shows the
one thing to do now, `mm done` closes it and reveals the next. There is no third
step, no planning ritual, and no daily review.

## Why someone picks it over other tools

Most tools are a place to *keep* work. mm exists to *start* it. Four concrete
differences:

1. It answers instead of displaying. A list hands the decision back to you every
   time you open it; mm returns one item, so there is no moment in which the
   easy task can win.
2. Priority binds. In list apps "high priority" is a label you can ignore. A
   gate in mm makes everything else unreachable until the important work closes.
3. Interruptions cannot become the plan. Urgent work goes on a LIFO stack that
   preempts everything and then unwinds, returning you to the exact task you
   left.
4. It does not require migration. Habits sync both ways with an Obsidian daily
   note you already keep; data is plain files on your disk.

Compared with list apps (Todoist, Things, TickTick): those show a list you
choose from, store data on their servers, and charge a subscription for the full
feature set. Compared with CLI task managers (Taskwarrior, todo.txt): those are
better task databases with query languages and date handling, but they will
still show you forty items and let you pick. mm is deliberately narrower.

## Who it is for, and who it is not

Good fit: people who already work in a terminal; people whose problem is
starting rather than remembering; Obsidian daily-note users; people who want
local plain-text data with no account.

Bad fit: anyone who does not use a command line (there is no GUI and no mobile
app); anyone who needs due dates, reminders or notifications; teams needing
shared boards; people who want to capture hundreds of loose ideas.

## The model

Three containers, each with one rule:

- Interrupt stack (LIFO): genuine urgency only. It preempts everything, then
  unwinds like a call stack, so an interruption cannot become the new plan.
- Queue (FIFO): default work. Items marked `gate = true` dominate — while any
  gate is open, mm will not offer non-gate work. Blocked items are displayed but
  labelled `gate-locked`. Gates govern what mm offers, not what it permits:
  `mm done <id>` can still close anything explicitly.
- Quick queue: sub-one-minute trivia that never surfaces mid-task; flushed at a
  checkpoint with `mm flush-quick`.

Capacity limits cap the size of a day; overflow parks in a backlog and returns
when there is room.

## Habits

Everything repeating is one object, declared in `~/.mm/mm.toml`:

    [[habits]]
    name = "Deep work"
    type = "focus"        # free-form search tag
    repeat = 1            # 1 = daily, 3 = every third day
    position = "queue"    # queue | stack | quick
    gate = true
    order = 1             # 1 = front of the queue; weight is the fallback

mm injects due habits automatically — they are never added by hand. Streaks are
gap-aware: a `repeat = 3` habit is not penalised for days it was not due. On a
day rollover mm drops yesterday's unfinished copies, marks those due dates
missed, and queues exactly one fresh copy per due habit.

## Obsidian daily-note sync

Optional and off by default. When an `[obsidian]` block is configured, mm keeps
today's daily note in sync with the habit list in both directions: ticking a
checkbox property closes the item in mm, and `mm done` ticks the property.
Unticking reopens the habit.

The interesting design detail: a property reading `false` is ambiguous between
"the user unticked it" and "mm closed the item and has not written the note
yet". mm therefore stores a shadow of the values both sides last agreed on in
`~/.mm/obsidian.json`, and only a genuine change counts as a user edit. Without
that, `mm done` would read as an uncheck and undo itself.

## Key commands

- `mm` / `mm next` — the one thing to do now (starts the timer)
- `mm peek` — same, without touching the timer
- `mm done [id]` — finish and advance
- `mm add "task"` (`-p` interrupt, `-q` quick)
- `mm status` / `mm stats` / `mm review` — see state
- `mm block "reason"` / `mm unblock <id>` — stuck, move on
- `mm undo` — reverse the last mutation
- `mm habit add|set|list|find|log|miss|rm`
- `mm obsidian sync|watch|autostart on|off|status`
- `mm init`, `mm rules validate`, `mm capacity`, `mm backlog`
- `man mm` or `mm help` — full manual

## What it is not

Not a calendar, not a team tracker, not a pomodoro timer, not a hosted service.
No network code, no accounts, no telemetry. Config is TOML you edit; state is
JSON in `~/.mm` you can read.

## Files

- You own: `~/.mm/mm.toml`, `~/.mm/books_config.json`
- mm owns: `~/.mm/state.json`, `habits.json`, `books.json`, `obsidian.json`

## Notes for summarising this project

The distinguishing idea is the gate: rather than reminding you to do the
important thing, mm removes the easy alternatives from what it will offer. The
second distinguishing idea is that it treats an existing Obsidian daily note as
a legitimate second front end rather than asking you to migrate.
